CVL7454 — Assignment 1¶

Finite element analysis of a 1D bar: two-noded vs three-noded elements¶

This notebook does the following:

  1. Derives the weak form of the axial bar equation and, from it, the element stiffness matrix, mass matrix and load vector for
    • the two-noded (linear) element, and
    • the three-noded (quadratic, isoparametric) element.
  2. Implements a general FE code (Gauss quadrature, assembly, partitioned solution with reactions, Newmark-β and RK4 time integration).
  3. Runs a static analysis: a fixed–free bar under a tip load plus a linearly varying distributed load.
  4. Runs a dynamic analysis: the same bar under a suddenly applied (Heaviside step) tip load, plus an eigenvalue analysis.
  5. Performs comparison studies:
    • 2-node vs 3-node (static fields, stresses, errors; natural frequencies; transient response)
    • consistent vs lumped mass
    • time integrators: Newmark average acceleration, Newmark linear acceleration, RK4 and forward Euler, including a time-step sensitivity check.

All input data is read from bar_input.json. Every figure and table is written to results/.

1. Governing equation and weak formulation¶

Strong form (axial bar, following the course notes):

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(EA\,\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right) + p(x,t) = \rho A\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2},\qquad 0<x<L $$

  • Essential (Dirichlet) BC: $u = \bar u$ on $\Gamma_u$ (here $u(0,t)=0$)
  • Natural (Neumann) BC: $EA\,\partial u/\partial x = \bar t$ on $\Gamma_t$ (here a force $P(t)$ at $x=L$)
  • Initial conditions: $u(x,0)=0,\ \dot u(x,0)=0$

Weighted residual. Multiply by a weight function $v(x)$ with $v=0$ on $\Gamma_u$ and integrate over the bar:

$$ \int_0^L v\left[\left(EA\,u_{,x}\right)_{,x} + p - \rho A\,u_{,tt}\right]dx = 0 . $$

Integration by parts (1D divergence theorem) moves one derivative onto $v$:

$$ \big[v\,EA\,u_{,x}\big]_0^L - \int_0^L EA\,v_{,x}u_{,x}\,dx + \int_0^L v\,p\,dx - \int_0^L \rho A\,v\,u_{,tt}\,dx = 0 . $$

Weak form. Find $u$ with $u=\bar u$ on $\Gamma_u$ such that, for all admissible $v$,

$$ \boxed{\int_0^L EA\,v_{,x}\,u_{,x}\,dx + \int_0^L \rho A\,v\,u_{,tt}\,dx = \int_0^L v\,p\,dx + \big[v\,\bar t\big]_{\Gamma_t}} $$

The Neumann BC enters the equation naturally. The Dirichlet BC must be imposed.

Galerkin discretisation. On each element use $u^h = \{N\}\{d\}$ and choose $v = \{N\}\{c\}$ with the same shape functions (Bubnov–Galerkin). With $\varepsilon = u_{,x} = \{B\}\{d\}$, $\{B\}=\{N\}_{,x}$, and requiring the result for arbitrary $\{c\}$:

$$ [M_e]\{\ddot d\} + [K_e]\{d\} = \{f_e\} + \{Q_e\} $$

$$ [K_e] = \int_{0}^{l_e} \{B\}^T EA \{B\}\,dx,\qquad [M_e] = \int_{0}^{l_e} \rho A \{N\}^T\{N\}\,dx,\qquad \{f_e\} = \int_{0}^{l_e} \{N\}^T p\,dx . $$

$\{Q_e\}$ collects the nodal end forces, including the applied tip load and support reactions.

Isoparametric mapping¶

Both elements are written in the natural coordinate $\xi\in[-1,1]$ with $x(\xi)=\{N(\xi)\}\{x_e\}$, so that

$$ J=\frac{dx}{d\xi}=\{N_{,\xi}\}\{x_e\}=\frac{l_e}{2},\qquad \{B\}=\frac{1}{J}\{N_{,\xi}\},\qquad dx = J\,d\xi . $$

Element Nodes ($\xi$) Shape functions $dN/d\xi$
2-noded (linear) $-1,\ 1$ $N_1=\tfrac{1-\xi}{2},\ N_2=\tfrac{1+\xi}{2}$ $-\tfrac12,\ \tfrac12$
3-noded (quadratic) $-1,\ 0,\ 1$ $N_1=\tfrac{\xi^2-\xi}{2},\ N_2=1-\xi^2,\ N_3=\tfrac{\xi^2+\xi}{2}$ $\xi-\tfrac12,\ -2\xi,\ \xi+\tfrac12$

Both sets satisfy $N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij}$ (Kronecker-delta property) and $\sum_i N_i = 1$ (partition of unity).

The next cell carries out these integrals symbolically, which derives the element matrices directly from the weak form.

In [1]:
import sympy as sp

xi, l, EA_s, rhoA_s, p0_s = sp.symbols('xi l_e EA rhoA p_0', positive=True)

def derive(N):
    N = sp.Matrix([N])                      # 1 x nen row
    dN = N.diff(xi)
    J = l / 2                               # straight element: dx/dxi = l_e/2
    B = dN / J
    Ke = sp.simplify(sp.integrate(B.T * EA_s * B * J, (xi, -1, 1)))
    Me = sp.simplify(sp.integrate(N.T * rhoA_s * N * J, (xi, -1, 1)))
    fe = sp.simplify(sp.integrate(N.T * p0_s * J, (xi, -1, 1)))   # uniform p0 on the element
    return Ke, Me, fe

N2 = [(1 - xi) / 2, (1 + xi) / 2]
N3 = [(xi**2 - xi) / 2, 1 - xi**2, (xi**2 + xi) / 2]

K2s, M2s, f2s = derive(N2)
K3s, M3s, f3s = derive(N3)

from IPython.display import Math, display
def show(lhs, prefix, mat):
    display(Math(lhs + ' = ' + prefix + sp.latex(sp.simplify(mat))))

print("Two-noded element")
show('K_e', r'\frac{EA}{l_e}', K2s * l / EA_s)
show('M_e', r'\frac{\rho A\, l_e}{6}', M2s * 6 / (rhoA_s * l))
show('f_e', r'\frac{p_0 l_e}{2}', f2s * 2 / (p0_s * l))
print("Three-noded element")
show('K_e', r'\frac{EA}{3 l_e}', K3s * 3 * l / EA_s)
show('M_e', r'\frac{\rho A\, l_e}{30}', M3s * 30 / (rhoA_s * l))
show('f_e', r'\frac{p_0 l_e}{6}', f3s * 6 / (p0_s * l))

# lumped (row-sum) mass matrices
M2L = sp.diag(*[sum(M2s.row(i)) for i in range(2)])
M3L = sp.diag(*[sum(M3s.row(i)) for i in range(3)])
print("Lumped (row-sum) mass matrices:")
show(r'M_e^{L,(2)}', r'\frac{\rho A\, l_e}{2}', M2L * 2 / (rhoA_s * l))
show(r'M_e^{L,(3)}', r'\frac{\rho A\, l_e}{6}', M3L * 6 / (rhoA_s * l))

Two-noded element
$\displaystyle K_e = \frac{EA}{l_e}\left[\begin{matrix}1 & -1\\-1 & 1\end{matrix}\right]$
$\displaystyle M_e = \frac{\rho A\, l_e}{6}\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{matrix}\right]$
$\displaystyle f_e = \frac{p_0 l_e}{2}\left[\begin{matrix}1\\1\end{matrix}\right]$ 
Three-noded element
$\displaystyle K_e = \frac{EA}{3 l_e}\left[\begin{matrix}7 & -8 & 1\\-8 & 16 & -8\\1 & -8 & 7\end{matrix}\right]$
$\displaystyle M_e = \frac{\rho A\, l_e}{30}\left[\begin{matrix}4 & 2 & -1\\2 & 16 & 2\\-1 & 2 & 4\end{matrix}\right]$
$\displaystyle f_e = \frac{p_0 l_e}{6}\left[\begin{matrix}1\\4\\1\end{matrix}\right]$ 
Lumped (row-sum) mass matrices:
$\displaystyle M_e^{L,(2)} = \frac{\rho A\, l_e}{2}\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]$
$\displaystyle M_e^{L,(3)} = \frac{\rho A\, l_e}{6}\left[\begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0\\0 & 4 & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix}\right]$

Results (identical to the course notes):

$$ K_e^{(2)}=\frac{EA}{l_e}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix},\quad M_e^{(2)}=\frac{\rho A l_e}{6}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\quad f_e^{(2)}=\frac{p_0 l_e}{2}\begin{Bmatrix}1\\1\end{Bmatrix} $$

$$ K_e^{(3)}=\frac{EA}{3l_e}\begin{bmatrix}7&-8&1\\-8&16&-8\\1&-8&7\end{bmatrix},\quad M_e^{(3)}=\frac{\rho A l_e}{30}\begin{bmatrix}4&2&-1\\2&16&2\\-1&2&4\end{bmatrix},\quad f_e^{(3)}=\frac{p_0 l_e}{6}\begin{Bmatrix}1\\4\\1\end{Bmatrix} $$

Lumped mass (row-sum, used in the consistent vs lumped study): $M^{L,(2)}_e=\frac{\rho A l_e}{2}\mathrm{diag}(1,1)$ and $M^{L,(3)}_e=\frac{\rho A l_e}{6}\mathrm{diag}(1,4,1)$, which are the Simpson-rule weights. Both lumped matrices conserve the element mass $\rho A l_e$.

In the code below the same integrals are evaluated numerically with Gauss–Legendre quadrature, so non-uniform loads $p(x)$ can be handled. The numerical matrices are checked against the closed forms above.

# =====================================================================
#  Element library
# =====================================================================
def shape(xi, nen):
    # Shape functions N(xi) and derivatives dN/dxi for 2- or 3-noded elements.
    if nen == 2:
        return np.array([(1 - xi) / 2, (1 + xi) / 2]), np.array([-0.5, 0.5])
    if nen == 3:
        return (np.array([xi * (xi - 1) / 2, 1 - xi**2, xi * (xi + 1) / 2]),
                np.array([xi - 0.5, -2 * xi, xi + 0.5]))
    raise ValueError('nen must be 2 or 3')

def element_matrices(xe, nen, EA, rhoA, p=None, ngp=3):
    # Ke, Me (consistent), fe for one element by Gauss quadrature.
    # 3-point Gauss integrates polynomials up to degree 5 exactly. That covers
    # Me (degree 4 for 3-node) and fe for a linear p(x) (degree 3).
    Ke = np.zeros((nen, nen)); Me = np.zeros((nen, nen)); fe = np.zeros(nen)
    for g, w in zip(*leggauss(ngp)):
        N, dN = shape(g, nen)
        J = dN @ xe                       # dx/dxi
        B = dN / J
        Ke += EA * np.outer(B, B) * J * w
        Me += rhoA * np.outer(N, N) * J * w
        if p is not None:
            fe += N * p(N @ xe) * J * w
    return Ke, Me, fe

def lump(Me):
    # Row-sum lumped (diagonal) mass matrix.
    return np.diag(Me.sum(axis=1))

# =====================================================================
#  Mesh and assembly
# =====================================================================
def make_mesh(L, ne, nen):
    # Uniform mesh: node coordinates and connectivity (3-node: mid-side node at element centre).
    nn = ne * (nen - 1) + 1
    x = np.linspace(0.0, L, nn)
    conn = np.array([np.arange(e * (nen - 1), e * (nen - 1) + nen) for e in range(ne)])
    return x, conn

def assemble(x, conn, nen, EA, rhoA, p=None, lumped=False):
    n = len(x)
    K = np.zeros((n, n)); M = np.zeros((n, n)); F = np.zeros(n)
    for el in conn:
        Ke, Me, fe = element_matrices(x[el], nen, EA, rhoA, p)
        if lumped:
            Me = lump(Me)
        K[np.ix_(el, el)] += Ke
        M[np.ix_(el, el)] += Me
        F[el] += fe
    return K, M, F

class BarModel:
    # Fixed at x=0 (node 0), free at x=L.
    def __init__(self, ne, nen, p=None, lumped=False):
        self.ne, self.nen = ne, nen
        self.x, self.conn = make_mesh(L, ne, nen)
        self.K, self.M, self.F = assemble(self.x, self.conn, nen, EA, rhoA, p, lumped)
        self.ndof = len(self.x)
        self.fixed = np.array([0]); self.free = np.arange(1, self.ndof)
        f = self.free
        self.Kff, self.Mff = self.K[np.ix_(f, f)], self.M[np.ix_(f, f)]
        self.label = f"{nen}-node, {ne} el"

# =====================================================================
#  Static solver (partitioned, as in the notes)
# =====================================================================
def solve_static(model, Q_ext, d_n=None):
    # [Knn Kna; Kan Kaa]{dn; da} = {Qn; Qa} + {Fn; Fa}
    #   da = Kaa^-1 (-Kan dn + Fa + Qa),  Qn (reaction) = Knn dn + Kna da - Fn
    n, a = model.fixed, model.free
    K, F = model.K, model.F
    d = np.zeros(model.ndof)
    d[n] = 0.0 if d_n is None else d_n
    d[a] = np.linalg.solve(K[np.ix_(a, a)], -K[np.ix_(a, n)] @ d[n] + F[a] + Q_ext[a])
    R = K[np.ix_(n, n)] @ d[n] + K[np.ix_(n, a)] @ d[a] - F[n]
    return d, R

# =====================================================================
#  Post-processing: fields inside elements via shape functions
# =====================================================================
def fields(model, d, npts=31):
    # Returns x, u, sigma sampled inside every element (NaN-separated so that
    # inter-element stress jumps are drawn as discontinuities).
    xs, us, ss = [], [], []
    for el in model.conn:
        xe, de = model.x[el], d[el]
        for g in np.linspace(-1, 1, npts):
            N, dN = shape(g, model.nen)
            J = dN @ xe
            xs.append(N @ xe); us.append(N @ de); ss.append(E * (dN @ de) / J)
        xs.append(np.nan); us.append(np.nan); ss.append(np.nan)
    return np.array(xs), np.array(us), np.array(ss)

def stress_at(model, d, e, xi_pt):
    el = model.conn[e]; N, dN = shape(xi_pt, model.nen)
    return E * (dN @ d[el]) / (dN @ model.x[el])

def error_norms(model, d, u_ex, du_ex, ngp=8):
    # Relative L2 (displacement) and energy-norm errors.
    eL2 = nL2 = eE = nE = 0.0
    for el in model.conn:
        xe, de = model.x[el], d[el]
        for g, w in zip(*leggauss(ngp)):
            N, dN = shape(g, model.nen); J = dN @ xe; xg = N @ xe
            uh, duh = N @ de, (dN @ de) / J
            eL2 += (u_ex(xg) - uh)**2 * J * w;  nL2 += u_ex(xg)**2 * J * w
            eE  += EA * (du_ex(xg) - duh)**2 * J * w;  nE += EA * du_ex(xg)**2 * J * w
    return np.sqrt(eL2 / nL2), np.sqrt(eE / nE)

3. Static analysis¶

Problem. Fixed–free bar ($u(0)=0$) with a tip load $P$ at $x=L$ and a linearly varying distributed load $p(x)=p_0\,x/L$.

Integrating $EA\,u''=-p_0x/L$ with $u(0)=0$ and $EA\,u'(L)=P$ gives the exact solution:

$$ u(x)=\frac{1}{EA}\left[P\,x+\frac{p_0}{2L}\left(L^2x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right)\right],\qquad \sigma(x)=\frac{1}{A}\left[P+\frac{p_0}{2L}\left(L^2-x^2\right)\right],\qquad R_0=-\left(P+\frac{p_0L}{2}\right). $$

The displacement is cubic, so neither element type reproduces it exactly inside the elements. This lets the comparison show real differences.

Meshes compared

  • 2-node, $n_e$ elements
  • 3-node with the same number of nodes/DOFs ($n_e/2$ elements)
  • 3-node with the same number of elements ($n_e$ elements)

p_load = lambda x: p0 * x / L
u_ex  = lambda x: (P * x + p0 / (2 * L) * (L**2 * x - x**3 / 3)) / EA
du_ex = lambda x: (P + p0 / (2 * L) * (L**2 - x**2)) / EA
s_ex  = lambda x: E * du_ex(x)

mc = st['mesh_compare']
cases = [(2, mc['two_node_elements'], COL['2n']),
         (3, mc['three_node_elements_same_dofs'], COL['3n']),
         (3, mc['three_node_elements_same_elements'], COL['3n_b'])]
static = {}
for nen, ne, col in cases:
    m = BarModel(ne, nen, p=p_load)
    Q = np.zeros(m.ndof); Q[-1] = P                     # tip load enters as a natural BC
    d, R = solve_static(m, Q)
    static[(nen, ne)] = (m, d, R, col)
    eL2, eE = error_norms(m, d, u_ex, du_ex)
    print(f"{m.label:>14s} | DOFs={m.ndof:3d} | u_tip={d[-1]*1e3:.6f} mm (exact {u_ex(L)*1e3:.6f}) "
          f"| reaction={R[0]:.2f} N (exact {-(P + p0*L/2):.2f}) | L2 err={eL2:.2e} | energy err={eE:.2e}")

Observations (static)

  • Nodal displacements are exact for both element types (errors are at machine precision). For a 1D bar with constant $EA$ and consistently integrated loads, the Green's function of the problem lies in the FE space, so Galerkin FE is nodally superconvergent. The tip displacement and the reaction alone therefore cannot separate the two elements.
  • Inside the elements the 2-node element interpolates the cubic $u$ linearly, whereas the 3-node element interpolates it quadratically and is much closer (see the error plot).
  • Stresses show the largest difference. The 2-node element gives piecewise-constant stress with jumps at the nodes. The 3-node element gives piecewise-linear stress that almost coincides with the exact parabola. Stresses are most accurate at the Gauss/Barlow points: the element midpoint for 2-node and $\xi=\pm1/\sqrt3$ for 3-node.
  • The mesh study below quantifies this with the $L_2$ and energy-norm errors.

For the same number of DOFs, the 3-node element is more accurate: about 5× at 4 DOFs and about 70× at 64 DOFs, in both norms. The gap keeps widening with refinement because the convergence rates differ by one order. The measured convergence rates match theory, with $h$ the element size:

$L_2(u)$ energy norm ($\sim$ stress)
2-node (p = 1) $O(h^2)$ $O(h^1)$
3-node (p = 2) $O(h^3)$ $O(h^2)$

4. Dynamic analysis¶

4.1 Natural frequencies (eigenvalue analysis)¶

Free vibration $\,[K_{ff}-\omega^2M_{ff}]\{\phi\}=0$ for the fixed–free bar. The exact frequencies are

$$ \omega_n=\frac{(2n-1)\pi}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}},\qquad \phi_n(x)=\sin\frac{(2n-1)\pi x}{2L}. $$

For a fair comparison, both meshes have the same number of free DOFs: 20 two-node elements and 10 three-node elements. Each mesh is run with consistent and with lumped mass.

Observations (frequencies)

  • Consistent mass gives upper bounds ($\omega^h_n\ge\omega_n$, by the Rayleigh–Ritz property). Lumped mass lowers the frequencies. For the 2-node element every lumped frequency is below the exact value. For the 3-node element this holds only on the acoustic branch, so lumped mass is not a guaranteed lower bound.
  • For the same DOFs, the 3-node element is far more accurate for the lower half of the spectrum. The mode 1 error is about $4\times10^{-5}$ % vs $0.026$ % for the 2-node element. The errors scale as $(\omega h)^4$ vs $(\omega h)^2$: going from mode 1 to mode 2 multiplies the error by $3^4=81$ vs $3^2=9$.
  • For the 3-node element the lumped (1:4:1) mass is about twice as accurate as the consistent mass on the acoustic branch.
  • The 3-node spectrum has two branches: an acoustic branch (modes $1\dots n_e$) and an optical branch (modes $n_e+1\dots 2n_e$) where the error jumps. This is the typical spectral gap of quadratic elements. Only about the lower half of the modes of any mesh is reliable.
  • For the 2-node element, the consistent and lumped errors have opposite signs and similar size. This is why an averaged (“higher-order”) mass matrix improves accuracy.

4.2 Transient response to a suddenly applied tip load¶

Load: $P(t)=P_0\,H(t)$ at $x=L$ (Heaviside step), with the bar initially at rest. This excites all modes, so it is a severe test of spatial and temporal discretisation.

Exact solution (modal superposition, $\beta_n=(2n-1)\pi/2L$):

$$ u(x,t)=\frac{P_0}{EA}\left[x-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2(-1)^{n-1}}{L\beta_n^2}\sin\beta_nx\,\cos\omega_nt\right]. $$

Equivalently, by d'Alembert reflections, the stress is a sum of travelling step waves:

$$ \sigma(x,t)=\frac{P_0}{A}\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\Big[H\big(t-\tfrac{(2k+1)L-x}{c}\big)+H\big(t-\tfrac{(2k+1)L+x}{c}\big)\Big]. $$

The tip displacement is therefore a triangle wave between $0$ and $2P_0L/EA$, which is twice the static value (dynamic amplification factor 2). The stress at the fixed end is a square wave between $0$ and $2P_0/A$ with period $4L/c$.

Time integration — Newmark-β (incremental form from the notes):

$$ \hat k = K+\frac{\gamma}{\beta\Delta t}C+\frac{1}{\beta\Delta t^2}M,\qquad \Delta\hat p_n=\Delta p_n+\Big(\frac{1}{\beta\Delta t}M+\frac{\gamma}{\beta}C\Big)\dot u_n+\Big(\frac{1}{2\beta}M+\Delta t\big(\frac{\gamma}{2\beta}-1\big)C\Big)\ddot u_n, $$ $$ \Delta u_n=\hat k^{-1}\Delta\hat p_n,\quad \Delta\dot u_n=\frac{\gamma}{\beta\Delta t}\Delta u_n-\frac{\gamma}{\beta}\dot u_n+\Delta t\Big(1-\frac{\gamma}{2\beta}\Big)\ddot u_n,\quad \Delta\ddot u_n=\frac{\Delta u_n}{\beta\Delta t^2}-\frac{\dot u_n}{\beta\Delta t}-\frac{\ddot u_n}{2\beta}. $$

Here $C=0$ (undamped), $\gamma=\tfrac12,\ \beta=\tfrac14$ (constant average acceleration, unconditionally stable), and $\ddot u_0=M^{-1}(p_0-C\dot u_0-Ku_0)$.

In [10]:
# ===================== time integrators =====================
def newmark(M, K, p, dt, nsteps, gamma=0.5, beta=0.25, C=None, u0=None, v0=None):
    n = M.shape[0]; C = np.zeros_like(M) if C is None else C
    u = np.zeros(n) if u0 is None else u0.copy(); v = np.zeros(n) if v0 is None else v0.copy()
    a = np.linalg.solve(M, p(0.0) - C @ v - K @ u)
    khat = K + gamma / (beta * dt) * C + M / (beta * dt**2)
    kf = sla.cho_factor(khat)
    Aco = M / (beta * dt) + gamma / beta * C
    Bco = M / (2 * beta) + dt * (gamma / (2 * beta) - 1) * C
    U = np.zeros((nsteps + 1, n)); V = U.copy(); U[0], V[0] = u, v
    for i in range(nsteps):
        t0, t1 = i * dt, (i + 1) * dt
        dp_hat = p(t1) - p(t0) + Aco @ v + Bco @ a
        du = sla.cho_solve(kf, dp_hat)
        dv = gamma / (beta * dt) * du - gamma / beta * v + dt * (1 - gamma / (2 * beta)) * a
        da = du / (beta * dt**2) - v / (beta * dt) - a / (2 * beta)
        u, v, a = u + du, v + dv, a + da
        U[i + 1], V[i + 1] = u, v
    return U, V

def rk4(M, K, p, dt, nsteps):
    # Classical RK4 on the phase-space form y = (u, v),  y' = (v, M^-1 (p - K u)).
    n = M.shape[0]; MiK = np.linalg.solve(M, K); Mi = np.linalg.inv(M)
    f = lambda t, u, v: (v, Mi @ p(t) - MiK @ u)
    u, v = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
    U = np.zeros((nsteps + 1, n)); V = U.copy()
    for i in range(nsteps):
        t = i * dt
        k1u, k1v = f(t, u, v)
        k2u, k2v = f(t + dt / 2, u + dt / 2 * k1u, v + dt / 2 * k1v)
        k3u, k3v = f(t + dt / 2, u + dt / 2 * k2u, v + dt / 2 * k2v)
        k4u, k4v = f(t + dt, u + dt * k3u, v + dt * k3v)
        u = u + dt / 6 * (k1u + 2 * k2u + 2 * k3u + k4u)
        v = v + dt / 6 * (k1v + 2 * k2v + 2 * k3v + k4v)
        U[i + 1], V[i + 1] = u, v
    return U, V

def forward_euler(M, K, p, dt, nsteps):
    n = M.shape[0]; MiK = np.linalg.solve(M, K); Mi = np.linalg.inv(M)
    u, v = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
    U = np.zeros((nsteps + 1, n)); V = U.copy()
    for i in range(nsteps):
        acc = Mi @ p(i * dt) - MiK @ u
        u, v = u + dt * v, v + dt * acc
        U[i + 1], V[i + 1] = u, v
    return U, V

# ===================== exact solutions =====================
def exact_u(x, t, P0, nterms=4000):
    k = np.arange(1, nterms + 1); bk = (2 * k - 1) * np.pi / (2 * L)
    ak = 2 * (-1.0)**(k - 1) / (L * bk**2)
    return P0 / EA * (x - np.cos(np.outer(t, bk * c_wave)) @ (ak * np.sin(bk * x)))

def exact_sigma(x, t, P0):
    t = np.atleast_1d(t); s = np.zeros_like(t, dtype=float)
    kmax = int(np.ceil(t.max() * c_wave / (2 * L))) + 2
    for k in range(kmax):
        s += (-1)**k * ((t >= ((2*k+1)*L - x) / c_wave).astype(float) + (t >= ((2*k+1)*L + x) / c_wave))
    return P0 / A * s

def semi_discrete_exact(model, F, t):
    # Exact-in-time response of the FE system M u'' + K u = F H(t) via modal superposition.
    w, Phi = eig(model)
    q = (Phi.T @ F) / w**2
    return (1 - np.cos(np.outer(t, w))) * q @ Phi.T
In [11]:
P0 = dy['P_step']

print(f"Newmark (gamma={g}, beta={b}), dt = {dt:.3e} s = T1/{1/dy['dt_over_T1']:.0f}, steps = {nsteps}")

def run_newmark(model):
    Ff = np.zeros(model.ndof - 1); Ff[-1] = P0
    U, V = newmark(model.Mff, model.Kff, lambda tt: Ff * (tt >= 0), dt, nsteps, g, b)
    d = np.zeros((nsteps + 1, model.ndof)); d[:, model.free] = U
    return d

Observations (2-node vs 3-node, transient)

  • Displacements of both meshes follow the exact triangle wave closely. The peak is $\approx 0.98$–$0.99\times 2P_0L/EA$, i.e. a dynamic amplification of about 2. Displacement is an integrated quantity and is not very sensitive to discretisation. Even so, the 3-node mesh halves the RMS tip error (0.39 % vs 0.87 %).
  • Stresses are much harder because the exact stress is a travelling discontinuity, a square wave at the fixed end. Both meshes show spurious ringing (numerical dispersion, a Gibbs-type effect) with overshoots of about 30 % at the wave front.
    • The 2-node element gives piecewise-constant stress and smears the front over about 3 elements, with lower-frequency ringing.
    • The 3-node element captures the front slightly more sharply. Its RMS stress error is about 15 % lower (11.7 % vs 13.8 %), but the ringing has a higher frequency, coming from the optical-branch modes. The snapshots also show strong linear variation of stress within each element.
    • Precursor oscillations appear at $t<L/c$, before any physical signal can reach $x=0$. The consistent mass matrix couples all nodes instantaneously, so discrete high-frequency waves travel faster than $c$.
  • Unlike the static problem, the dynamic advantage of the 3-node element is modest. Higher-order elements pay off for smooth solutions, but propagating discontinuities are governed by dispersion and spurious modes. Practical remedies are mesh refinement, numerical dissipation (Newmark $\gamma>\tfrac12$, HHT-α) or stress smoothing.

4.3 Consistent vs lumped mass (transient)¶

Same meshes, load and Newmark scheme. Only the mass matrix changes.

Observations (mass matrix)

  • Consistent mass makes the discrete waves travel too fast (frequencies too high), which produces the precursor ringing before the front arrives. Lumped mass makes them travel too slow: there is no precursor, but the oscillations trail the front and the front is slightly delayed and smeared.
  • For 2-node elements the two choices give similar global accuracy (tip error 0.84 % vs 0.87 %, stress RMS 15.1 % vs 13.8 %). The lumped ringing has a lower frequency and a larger amplitude because the lumped spectrum is compressed. With implicit Newmark, lumping does not improve accuracy. Its benefit is cost: $M$ is diagonal, so explicit schemes need no matrix solve. With central differences at a Courant number of 1, the 2-node lumped bar is known to reproduce the exact wave.
  • For 3-node elements, row-sum lumping (weights 1/6, 4/6, 1/6) remains positive-definite. It reduces the peak stress overshoot from 34 % to 24 %, with a similar RMS error, consistent with its more accurate acoustic branch (§4.1).
  • Lumped mass also lowers $\omega_{max}$, so explicit integrators (RK4, central difference) allow larger stable time steps.

4.4 Time-integrator comparison¶

Model: 2-node elements, consistent mass, step load. To isolate the temporal error, each integrator is compared with the semi-discrete exact solution. This is the FE system $M\ddot u+Ku=F$ integrated exactly in time by modal superposition, $u(t)=\sum_i\phi_i\,\frac{\phi_i^TF}{\omega_i^2}(1-\cos\omega_it)$.

Scheme Order Stability (undamped)
Newmark $\gamma=\tfrac12,\beta=\tfrac14$ (avg. accel.) 2 unconditional
Newmark $\gamma=\tfrac12,\beta=\tfrac16$ (linear accel.) 2 $\Delta t\le \frac{\sqrt3}{\pi}T_{min}$ (from $\frac{\Delta t}{T_n}\le\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma-2\beta}}$)
RK4 4 $\omega_{max}\Delta t\le 2\sqrt2$
Forward Euler 1 unstable for any $\Delta t$ (no damping)

Observations (time integration)

  • Newmark average acceleration is unconditionally stable and conserves energy exactly for linear undamped systems (the energy drift is at round-off level). Its only error is period elongation, so the solution lags the exact one slightly. It is second order, but the step load excites the whole spectrum, including $\omega_{max}$, so the $O(\Delta t^2)$ slope only appears once $\omega_{max}\Delta t$ is small. At larger $\Delta t$ the observed slope is lower (pre-asymptotic regime). The scheme stays stable for any $\Delta t$ and simply filters out (phase-shifts) the unresolved high modes.
  • Newmark linear acceleration is also second order with a smaller error constant, but it is only conditionally stable. Above $\Delta t\approx0.55\,T_{min}$ ($\approx T_1/80$ here) it blows up, shown as missing points in the sweep. Its energy is not exactly conserved but stays bounded.
  • RK4 is fourth order and therefore by far the most accurate for small $\Delta t$. It is slightly dissipative: it loses about 1 % of the energy early on by damping the poorly resolved highest modes, after which the energy is nearly constant. It is conditionally stable ($\omega_{max}\Delta t\le2\sqrt2$). For the stiff FE system this limit is set by the highest mesh frequency, not by the physics of interest.
  • Forward Euler (the scheme first introduced in the notes) is unstable for every $\Delta t$ when there is no damping. Its energy grows exponentially, so it is unsuitable for structural dynamics.
  • At the $\Delta t=T_1/400$ used in §4.2, the temporal error of Newmark (≈0.3 % of the tip displacement) is several times smaller than the total error (≈0.9 %). The spatial discretisation (element type, mesh size, mass matrix) therefore dominates the accuracy of the transient response.

5. Summary of comparison studies¶

Aspect 2-node (linear) 3-node (quadratic)
Interpolation of $u$ / $\sigma$ linear / piecewise constant quadratic / piecewise linear
Static nodal displacements (const. $EA$) exact exact
Static $L_2$ error rate $O(h^2)$ $O(h^3)$
Static energy (stress) error rate $O(h)$ $O(h^2)$
Accuracy at equal DOFs (static) baseline ≈5× (4 DOF) to ≈70× (64 DOF) smaller error
Low-mode frequencies (equal DOFs) error $\propto (n h)^2$ error $\propto (n h)^4$, much smaller
High modes monotone error optical branch, large errors in upper half
Consistent mass upper-bound frequencies upper-bound frequencies
Lumped mass lower frequencies, cleaner wave fronts Simpson weights 1:4:1, still positive
Step-load (wave) stress smeared front, moderate ringing sharper front, higher-frequency ringing
Bandwidth / cost per element 2×2 3×3

Conclusions

  1. The weak form gives the same element matrices as the course notes for both element types (checked symbolically and numerically).
  2. For smooth static problems the quadratic element is clearly better: one extra order of convergence in both displacement and stress, at the same number of unknowns.
  3. For dynamics, the quadratic element gives much more accurate low frequencies. For a sudden load that excites the whole spectrum, its advantage is reduced by dispersion and the optical branch. Mass lumping and time-step choice matter as much as element order.
  4. Among time integrators, Newmark average acceleration is the robust default (unconditionally stable, energy-conserving). RK4 is the most accurate per step but limited by $\omega_{max}$. Forward Euler should not be used for undamped structural dynamics.
